Demolition teams arrived to tear down Ruiz's residence as part of a project for ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition." "When Ty Pennington came to our home and said, 'Ruiz family, come on out,' we all just ran out and couldn't believe that we were chosen," Ruiz recalled. "It's a blessing to us, but we weren't expecting all of this at all, and it has been overwhelming."

Show host Pennington explained that among thousands of Texas applicants, the production team chose Ruiz's family specifically to provide her with something essential: better resources to expand her charitable efforts.

## Balancing Community Work and Personal Sacrifice

Beyond her regular deliveries to Juarez, Ruiz's family has been working to finish a facility there that will house a communal kitchen, an orphanage, and a vocational school.

This dedication came at a cost — the family had paused construction on their own house back in 1996 to focus on the Juarez community, according to Ruiz, resulting in an unfinished home. Compounding matters, much of their living quarters had turned into storage space for donations intended for Juarez residents.

"A home is somewhere you can go after a long day's work and relax and where the family can get together and be able to sit down and talk about our day," Ruiz explained. "When we had the things in the living room, we couldn't do that there."

## The Big Reveal

When the family returned from their Bahamas trip, a massive crowd of volunteers and neighbors gathered around them, using the production's oversized bus to hide the renovated home from view. After everyone shouted the show's signature phrase — "Move that bus!" — the Ruiz family finally saw their transformed residence.

"For us, it is a new beginning, and it's going to change our lives," Ruiz said.

## Expanding the Mission

This upgraded home means Ruiz can broaden the scope of her charitable work. Executive Producer Anthony Dominici noted that the renovation included a supplementary kitchen and extra storage space specifically designed for her mission.

Additionally, community generosity resulted in enough donated goods — food, clothing, and toys — to fill both a 20-foot shipping container and a 16-foot cube truck, including over 75,000 canned food items, according to Dominici.

"That's the whole point here," Pennington said. "To give her what she needs to make her life easier to literally spread dreams and hope to people who have absolutely none of either one of those."

## Background

Ruiz first gained international recognition when "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" aired on Thanksgiving across CNN's global networks. Actress Selena Gomez presented her with the CNN Hero honor, which came with a $25,000 award given to each of the year's top 10 honorees.

For more than 12 years, Maria Ruiz has dedicated her life to serving impoverished children and families across the border in Juarez, Mexico. Her tireless efforts—delivering food, clothing, and toys to those in need—have not gone unnoticed. In recognition of her extraordinary commitment to humanitarian service, Ruiz was honored as a CNN Hero, a title reserved for everyday individuals making an extraordinary difference in their communities.

Now, her selfless work has earned her family an extraordinary surprise. ABC's popular television program "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition" selected the Ruiz family for one of its signature transformations. # El Paso, Texas: A Border City in the National Spotlight

El Paso, Texas, sits at the westernmost tip of the state, sharing an international border with Ciudad Juárez, Mexico. This desert city, home to over 680,000 residents, has long been a vital crossing point for trade, culture, and immigration between the United States and Mexico. Its unique position has made it a frequent subject of national news coverage, particularly from major outlets like CNN.

CNN has covered El Paso extensively over the years, especially in relation to immigration policy and border security—topics that consistently dominate American political discourse. The city has served as a backdrop for reporting on migrant caravans, asylum-seeking families, and the various policy shifts enacted by different presidential administrations. Reporters and camera crews stationed along the Rio Grande have documented both the humanitarian challenges and the logistical complexities of managing a major international border crossing.

The city gained tragic national attention in August 2019, when a mass shooting at a Walmart store killed 23 people in what was investigated as a racially motivated attack targeting the Hispanic community. CNN, along with other major networks, provided extensive coverage of the tragedy, the community's response, and the broader national conversation about hate crimes and gun violence that followed.

Beyond crisis coverage, El Paso represents a unique binational metropolitan area where two countries, cultures, and economies intersect daily. Its story—as told through outlets like CNN—reflects broader national conversations about immigration, security, and the complex realities of life along America's southern border. The city continues to navigate its identity as both a distinctly Texan community and a bridge between two nations.

# Community Advocate's Dream Home Realized After Years of Service to Others

**LOS ANGELES** — For nearly two decades, Maria Ruiz opened the door of her modest three-bedroom house to any child in her East Los Angeles neighborhood who needed a warm meal, a safe place to do homework, or simply someone who cared. Now, thanks to a national television program, that door leads into a completely transformed home built specifically to support the after-school program she has run out of her living room since 2006.

Ruiz, 54, was named a CNN Hero in 2022 for founding "Manos Que Ayudan" (Helping Hands), a grassroots organization that provides free tutoring, meals, and mentorship to more than 200 children annually in one of Los Angeles' most underserved communities. Her story caught the attention of producers at ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition," which revived the beloved series last year with a mission to honor everyday heroes making an outsized impact.

"I never thought something like this could happen to someone like me," Ruiz said, fighting back tears as she stood before her new home for the first time. "I just wanted to help kids. I never imagined the world would want to help me back."

The transformation took just seven days, with more than 300 volunteers, local contractors, and construction crews working around the clock. Ruiz and her family were sent on an all-expenses-paid trip to Hawaii while the work was completed — a tradition that has become a hallmark of the show since its original run from 2003 to 2012.

The new home now includes a dedicated tutoring center with individual study pods, a industrial-grade kitchen where volunteers can prepare meals for dozens of children at once, a computer lab stocked with donated laptops, and a rooftop garden where kids in the program learn about sustainable agriculture.

"Maria has been quietly changing lives in this neighborhood for 18 years without asking for anything in return," said Ty Pennington, who returned to host the rebooted series. "The least we could do was give her the space to keep doing what she does best — except now she won't have kids doing homework on her kitchen floor."

Neighbors and former program participants lined the streets during the home's unveiling, many holding signs thanking Ruiz for her impact on their lives.

Carlos Mendoza, 22, credits Ruiz's program with keeping him on track during a difficult adolescence after his father was deported. "Miss Maria fed me dinner probably 500 times," Mendoza said. "She helped me with college applications when nobody else would. This is the least she deserves."

CNN's Heroes program, now in its 18th year, has honored hundreds of everyday individuals making extraordinary contributions to their communities worldwide. Ruiz was among 10 honorees recognized during the annual "CNN Heroes: An All-Star Tribute" broadcast, which raises awareness and funding for grassroots organizations often overlooked by larger philanthropic efforts.

"What strikes me about Maria's story is that she never sought recognition," said Anderson Cooper, who has hosted the CNN Heroes tribute for over a decade. "She was simply doing the work because she saw a need. That's the common thread among all our Heroes — and it's exactly why they deserve to be seen."

Ruiz says the expanded space will allow her to nearly double the number of children she can serve, and she's already fielding calls from local school counselors eager to refer additional families.

"This house isn't really mine," Ruiz said, looking around at the new facility bearing her program's name in bright letters above the entrance. "It belongs to every kid who walks through that door looking for a little hope."

Manos Que Ayudan continues to accept donations and volunteers through its website, with Ruiz noting that the physical space, however improved, remains secondary to the mission that built it.

"The walls are new," she said, "but the heart of this place has always been the same."

# Juarez Humanitarian Worker Gets Emotional Surprise: A New Home From TV Crew

**JUAREZ, Mexico** — For nearly two decades, Maria Elena Rodriguez has given everything she has to help others. Now, a television show has given something back.

Rodriguez, 54, has spent 18 years running a modest shelter out of her own home in Juarez, providing food, clothing and temporary refuge to migrants, families fleeing violence, and neighbors who had nowhere else to turn. She did it all while living in a crumbling two-bedroom house with a leaking roof and walls held together, she says, "by prayer and duct tape."

That home is now gone — replaced by a newly built house courtesy of a home makeover television crew that spent months planning the surprise in secret.

"I still don't believe it," Rodriguez said Tuesday, standing in the doorway of her new kitchen, tears streaming down her face. "I keep thinking I'm going to wake up."

## A Life of Service

Neighbors describe Rodriguez as a fixture in the community — the woman who never turned anyone away, even when it meant her own family went without.

"She would give her last tortilla to a stranger," said Carlos Mendoza, a local pastor who has worked alongside Rodriguez for over a decade. "This woman has slept on the floor so that others could have a bed. She deserves this and so much more."

Rodriguez's shelter has assisted thousands of people over the years, according to local organizers, particularly during recent surges in migration through the border region. Her work often went unpaid and unrecognized — until producers from the television program heard her story through a local nonprofit and decided to act.

## The Surprise

Production crews spent nearly three months quietly constructing the new home on the same lot, all while Rodriguez believed she was participating in a documentary about humanitarian work along the border.

"We had to get creative keeping her away from the site," said the show's lead producer, who asked that the program not be named ahead of its official air date. "But when we finally brought her back and she saw it for the first time — that's the moment we do this for."

Video from the reveal shows Rodriguez collapsing to her knees in the front yard, surrounded by neighbors, volunteers and members of her family who had flown in for the occasion.

The new home includes a reinforced roof, updated plumbing and electrical systems, and — most importantly to Rodriguez — a dedicated space downstairs that will continue to serve as an intake area for those seeking help.

"They didn't just build me a house," Rodriguez said. "They built me a bigger way to keep doing what I love."

## What's Next

Rodriguez says she has no plans to slow down. If anything, she says, the new space will allow her to help more people than ever before.

"This isn't the end of anything," she said. "It's just a stronger foundation for the work God has given me."

The episode featuring Rodriguez's story is expected to air later this year.

# From Modest Beginnings to Dream Home: El Paso's Maria Ruiz Gets Life-Changing Surprise

**EL PASO, Texas (CNN)** — For nearly two decades, Maria Ruiz has opened the door of her modest home to children who had nowhere else to go. Now, thanks to a community-driven effort and a surprise that left her speechless, Ruiz has a new door to open — one leading into a custom-built house designed specifically for the work she's dedicated her life to.

Ruiz, who was honored as a CNN Hero for her tireless work providing shelter, food and stability to at-risk youth in this border city, has spent years operating out of a cramped, aging house that also served as a makeshift shelter for the children under her care. Neighbors say the modest home's plumbing frequently failed and there was never quite enough space for everyone who needed it.

"She never once complained," said longtime neighbor Estella Marquez. "Even when the roof leaked or the heater broke in the middle of winter, Maria made sure the kids were warm and fed first. She always said her needs came last."

That selflessness is part of what caught the attention of CNN, which recognized Ruiz among its annual CNN Heroes — a program celebrating everyday people making extraordinary differences in their communities. Her nomination highlighted years of work housing displaced and vulnerable children in El Paso, often relying on her own limited income and donations from neighbors to keep the lights on.

The recognition set off a chain of events that culminated this month in a dramatic home renovation, spearheaded by a team of builders, designers and volunteers who worked around the clock to construct a new home suited to Ruiz's mission — one with additional bedrooms, a larger kitchen, and safety features designed with children in mind.

Television personality and carpenter Ty Pennington, known for his work on ABC's "Extreme Makeover: Home Edition," lent his voice to celebrate Ruiz's transformation, calling her "the definition of a hero."

"Maria didn't build a shelter — she built a family," Pennington said. "This home isn't just walls and a roof. It's a place where kids who've been overlooked their whole lives finally get to feel like they matter. That's what community looks like."
